**Introducing Goldleaf: money that grows on trees**

For most of modern history, money arrived from somewhere else: a bank, an employer, a central authority. When those authorities could no longer stand behind their currencies, the arrangement failed almost overnight. In many places, what replaced it was Goldleaf: money that grows on trees.

It began as a stopgap for local exchange, a way for neighbours to issue money with their own hands, on a windowsill, in a garden, across an orchard. Early accounts describe Saturday markets where people arrived with seedlings in yoghurt pots and margarine tubs, each labelled in biro with its lineage, and haggled over a cutting the way their parents had haggled over change.

None of this was quite new. Towns had issued their own money before, from the [stamped scrip of Wörgl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miracle_of_W%C3%B6rgl) in the Austrian depression of 1932 to the [Lewes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewes_Pound), [Brixton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brixton_Pound) and [Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Pound) pounds of the early twenty-first century. What was new was a currency that nobody could print and everybody could check.

The barter spread from town to town as lineages were shared and recognised. Within three growing seasons, one survey counted around 40,000 registered plants across some 200 towns. Within a decade, regional orchards of a few thousand trees each were backing a plurality of currencies traded across borders, the competing private monies Friedrich Hayek had imagined in [*The Denationalisation of Money*](https://iea.org.uk/publications/research/denationalisation-of-money/), though rooted in soil rather than banks.

The idea underneath is simple to state. Value is stored in a plant’s DNA, and growing, tending and harvesting the plant are how money is issued. A grower’s morning round of watering and pinching out is, quite literally, bookkeeping.

The design borrows from several places. From Satoshi Nakamoto’s [2008 bitcoin paper](https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf) it takes the chain of records, each pointing to the one before, so that history cannot be quietly rewritten. From gold it takes scarcity that nobody can decree. From horticulture it takes four centuries of [grafting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grafting), and from [modern monetary theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_monetary_theory), as set out by economists such as Stephanie Kelton, the view that money is a social arrangement whose supply can be managed in the public interest.

The storage itself rests on a line of laboratory work that once looked like a curiosity. In 2012 George Church’s group at Harvard [wrote a whole book into synthetic DNA](https://wyss.harvard.edu/news/writing-the-book-in-dna/). In 2013 Nick Goldman’s team at the European Bioinformatics Institute [stored Shakespeare’s sonnets](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature11875) and a recording of Martin Luther King’s “I have a dream” speech. In 2017 Church’s lab used CRISPR to [write a short film into the genomes of living bacteria](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature23017), frames of a galloping horse after [Eadweard Muybridge’s photographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Horse_in_Motion), and read it back after the cells had multiplied. Goldleaf moved that idea out of the bacterium and into the orchard.

Each plant line carries a genetic ledger: short synthetic sequences written into [intergenic regions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intergenic_region), the stretches between genes that the plant does not use to make proteins. Each record is flanked by marker sequences, so it can be found without reading the whole genome. Every record holds a parent hash, a lineage identifier, a harvest count and an error-correcting checksum, and like a block in a chain it points back to the plant it came from.

The cutting is what makes this work. An apple grown from a pip is a genetic stranger to both its parents, which is why every named variety, from Bramley to Cox, has been kept going for centuries by grafting rather than by seed. A grafted tree is a clone, and a clone carries its ledger forward intact.

Clones are not perfect copies, though. Orchardists have long known the occasional branch that comes out different, a [*sport*](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_(botany)>), and many famous varieties began that way. Because DNA copies itself with the occasional mistake, each record is stored at several loci and reconciled by majority when read, the same principle, known as [triple modular redundancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_modular_redundancy), that engineers use to keep spacecraft computers running through radiation.

New money comes through *proof of growth*. A harvest is a claim to mint, and it becomes valid once independent sequencers attest that the tissue carries a record descending from a known lineage, with a harvest count one higher than its parent’s.

Bitcoin issues new coins through [*proof of work*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_work): miners burn electricity solving arbitrary puzzles, and the cost of the energy is what makes the coins scarce. Goldleaf swaps the puzzle for an orchard. Time, care and sunlight do the work, and the energy spent is mostly the sun’s.

A typical apple lineage yields its first mintable harvest after four or five years, which is why older growers talk about trees the way their parents talked about pensions.

Anyone with a sequencer can check a leaf, with no bank in the loop. The portable [nanopore sequencers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanopore_sequencing) of the 2010s were already the size of a stapler; their descendants sit in the post office or the pub, and a reading takes about twenty minutes.

Supply follows the seasons, so most regions see 60 to 70 percent of a year’s new money arrive in a few weeks of autumn. That would have pleased [Silvio Gesell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silvio_Gesell), whose ideas inspired the Wörgl scrip, and who argued that money should behave more like the goods it buys, which rot, rust and come in harvests. Consensus is slow by design. It moves at the speed of seasons, not seconds.

The machinery around the plants is ordinary. Sequencers, attestations and the shared index of lineages all run on the stored-program design John von Neumann sketched in his [1945 report on the EDVAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Draft_of_a_Report_on_the_EDVAC), in which instructions and data share one memory and run step by step. To those machines the plant is a peripheral: a slow, durable, tamper-evident storage device. Reading a leaf is an I/O operation; verifying it is hashing and comparison.

Inside the plant, things are different. There is no clock, no separation of memory and processor, no sequential stream of instructions. Every cell copies the ledger at once, and mutation behaves less like a bug than like the noise that [stochastic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_computing) and [analogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analog_computer) computing learn to tolerate. Goldleaf lives on that boundary, using familiar machines to interpret a medium that computes on its own terms.

That boundary is also where the trouble came. The obvious attacks arrived early. Forgers synthesised DNA and inserted plausible records into new plants, thieves took cuttings from other people’s orchards, and on older lines the records slowly drifted as sports and small mutations piled up.

Each found its answer. Claims now need attestations from several independent sequencers, so that a minority of corrupt or careless ones cannot outvote the rest; computer scientists know this as the [Byzantine generals problem](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/byzantine-generals-problem/), after a 1982 paper by Leslie Lamport and colleagues. Lineages are bound to registered growers, so a stolen cutting mints nothing for the thief. Lines whose records fall below a fidelity threshold are retired, their value carried into a successor.

Less expected were the birds. Pips eaten in one orchard were dropped in another parish’s hedgerow, and within a few years wild seedlings were turning up on verges and railway embankments. Being grown from seed rather than grafted, each was a cross between two lineages and carried fragments of both ledgers.

After a winter of disputes, most federations settled on treating self-sown trees as common money, minted for the parish whose land they grow on. The rules they drew up read much like the principles [Elinor Ostrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom) found in centuries-old village commons: clear boundaries, local monitoring and penalties that start small. Some of the best-loved currencies now draw a share of their supply from hedgerows nobody planted.

Then there was scale. If money is grown, what stops an agribusiness from simply planting more of it than everyone else? Because each mintable harvest needs years of tending and its own attestation, a thousand-hectare estate cannot print money any faster than its trees mature, though it can certainly print more of it.

So regional federations of growers came to act as something like central banks. They cap how many new lineages any one grower may register each season, and they can raise the number of attestations a large harvest needs, slowing issuance when one estate threatens to dominate a currency.

The harder lesson came from the estates that tried to outgrow those rules. In the first boom, several engineered fast-maturing lineages, bred for early mintable harvests and planted in vast clonal blocks kept alive by heavy insecticide spraying. For a few seasons they out-issued everyone.

History had already shown how this ends. [Ireland’s potatoes in the 1840s](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Famine_(Ireland)>) and the [Gros Michel banana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gros_Michel_banana) a century later were each a single vulnerable variety grown at vast scale, and each was cut down by one disease. So it went again. The [pollinators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pollinator_decline) around the estates collapsed, a single fungal strain moved through the identical trees, and whole currencies lost a third of their supply in one summer.

The fix came from the growers rather than the estates. Federations began weighting attestations by the genetic diversity of the orchard a harvest came from, refused to register lineages whose maturation had been artificially shortened, and required sequencers to flag pesticide residues, which void a claim to mint.

Within a few years the cheapest way to issue money was to keep a varied, living, insect-friendly orchard, and the monocultures quietly went back to being farms.

Plenty is still argued over in pub back rooms and federation minutes. Sequencing keeps getting faster but is not yet cheap enough for everyday payments, so small change still tends to move as signed chits against a coming harvest.

Nobody has settled whether a cross-pollinated tree merges two ledgers or forks them, in the sense a [blockchain forks](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fork_(blockchain)>) when its users disagree, or what becomes of the value when a lineage dies out. There is a standing quarrel over whether the estates should play by the same rules as the allotments, or answer to something closer to the old central authority.

And beneath the technical questions sit the older ones that a global economy rooted in orchards still has to answer: who tends the trees, what happens in a drought, and what it means to plant savings for your grandchildren.

Picture an October morning in a village where the post office sequencer has a queue out the door. A girl carries a basket of windfalls from the tree her grandmother planted the year she was born; that tree is her university fund.

The bees are loud in the hedgerows because nobody sprays them any more, and the talk in the queue is of rainfall, soil and which old varieties are coming back.

Nobody here is blind to nature, because nobody can afford to be: the health of the land is the health of the money, and everyone can read both. It is not a perfect economy, but it is one that grows more beautiful the more carefully it is kept.

*The above describes a speculative future monetary protocol and its impacts.*
